comments.author: tywr
comments.text:
Wow, I didn't really expect to see my project there this morning! I'm normally a simple lurker, but I wanted to say thanks for the kind words about the project.

I know some people might want to modify or tweak the project to their liking. The project is meant to provide a Python sandbox more than just font files, so feel free to fork it or submit a PR if you feel like some glyphs need tweaking! You don't need any external tools to draw/visualize the glyphs.

What I really want is a hand anti-aliased bitmap font which prioritizes sharpness.

comments.author: jan_m_savage
comments.text:
It's a bit like the paid font Berkeley Mono which I've been using for a while now. But I think Nordwand feels softer and nicer, it embodies a message in the font (thus the fluency effect is more potent).

The message may be subjective but it strikes me as: "I, the font, contain important data [due to the sharp curvatures and uniform size of letter elements]. Not sure if others think about fonts in this way.

Berkeley Mono's message to me feels like "I'm just doing my job, don't mind me, focus on your thing".

comments.author: kqr
comments.text:
I have been going back and forth between Luxi Mono (serif monospace fonts are rare but look great on high-resolution monitors) and Hack (like Helvetica, it has virtually no personality and thus fits well everywhere). Everything else I've seen has looked... weird or off somehow. But this is one of the first alternatives I'm entertaining the idea of trying.

My main concern is that the tall glyphs for less than < and greater than > will disambiguate badly with actual Unicode left 〈 and right angle brackets 〉.

Edit: I also realised just now the ASCII hyphen-minus - is quite long with this typeface, which makes it ambiguous with the longer dashes. (It looks freakin' great in pure ASCII environments, though!)

comments.author: dancek
comments.text:
Thanks for mentioning it! First time I heard about Commit Mono. The first paragraph already had me wondering how a monospace font can read this well.

Turns out it has smart kerning, ie. character positions are subtly adjusted to compensate for different character widths. For example, i is narrow and m is wide. That causes words like "commit" to look bad in standard monospace fonts. The m's in the middle are very densely spaced and there are wide gaps around the i.

I'll be testing Commit Mono in my editors. Maybe it will even make me switch SilverBullet back to a monospace config.

input.title: Nordwand Mono – A monospace font for coders and adventurers

fast.overview: Discussion of Nordwand Mono, a new open-source monospace font for coding and terminal use, mostly comparing it to existing programming fonts.

points.text: Several commenters see strong resemblance to other fonts: one says it is basically JetBrains Mono, another says its overall shape resembles Berkeley Mono, while one commenter judges Berkeley Mono's feel differently.

One user worried the tall angle brackets and long hyphen may be ambiguous; another noted the hyphen matches the em dash width and the $ lacks a full vertical stroke, so it was not right for daily use.
Readability concerns included confusing 8 and 0 at small sizes, and parentheses and square brackets looking too similar, which one user said would increase cognitive load.

thorough.overview: Discussion of Nordwand Mono, a new open-source monospace coding font, comparing it to existing fonts and noting readability and glyph concerns.

points.text: Many commenters compare it to Berkeley Mono for its overall shape; one sees Ubuntu Mono in some glyphs ('m', '0'), and one says it looks like JetBrains Mono.
One commenter calls it 99% JetBrains Mono, though a comparison shows more differences; another says similar-looking fonts can still differ, as Arial and Verdana do.
Parentheses and square brackets look too similar, which could add cognitive load when coding.
Glyph concerns: the tall angle brackets may be ambiguous with Unicode angle brackets, and the hyphen is as wide as the em dash. The $ lacks a through-line.
A reader with aging eyes wants 8 and 0 to differ more in monospace fonts, since they confuse them at small sizes.
Only two ligatures are exposed, '->' and '=>', which pleases one commenter who dislikes ligatures like '=='. Ligatures can be removed from fonts with fontforge.
Some prefer bitmap fonts for sharpness and density, even on high-resolution screens; Cozette and hand-hinted Pragmata Pro are suggested.
One user cannot use it as a terminal font because it lacks characters they need.
